_comment: Policy for the Credentials Expiry Review workflow. Loaded at run time via the DownloadTemplate sub-workflow (template_name: datasets/credential_expiry.json), so edits here take effect on the next run without touching the workflow. Keys are consumed by parse_expiry_config.
_comment_no_inventory: There is deliberately no list of credentials in this file. n8n never returns an expiry date over its API - credential data is redacted on every path and oauthTokenData is blanked outright - so the date has to be written by a human somewhere. Writing it here would mean a second copy of your credential list that goes stale the moment one is renamed, added or deleted. Instead the date goes in the credential's own name in n8n, where it sits next to the thing it describes and is visible in the credentials list: "GitHub PAT (expires 2026-08-01)", "Token API cliente (caduca 2026-09-15)". This file only says how to recognise such a date and when to shout about it.
_comment_expirable_type_patterns: The only credential types in this instance that can expire, listed explicitly rather than guessed by pattern. linkedInOAuth2Api: n8n's own credential wizard says "access tokens valid for 60 days and do not return a refresh token". gmailOAuth2 and googleSheetsOAuth2Api: Google refresh tokens are revocable, die when the account password changes, and last only 7 days while the OAuth app sits in Testing mode. Everything else here is a plain API key with no expiry - valid until revoked, which is not a date. Add a type only when something documents that it expires, and give it a probe node in the workflow at the same time, or it will be chased for a date nothing can verify.
_comment_probes: Each expirable type has its own node in the workflow (probe_linkedin, probe_gmail, probe_google_sheets) that makes a real request to the provider with that credential. That is the only mechanism that detects an expired token: n8n's own test for OAuth types just checks that an access_token is stored, and no endpoint exposes the expiry. Probe verdicts outrank dates in both directions - a token the provider rejects is EXPIRED whatever its name says, and a token that still answers is not expired just because a derived date ran out. 403 and 404 count as alive, because the request authenticated before the provider objected to the scope or the path. 429 and 5xx are inconclusive and stay silent. Adding a type here without adding its probe node leaves it dated but unverified.
_comment_test_type_patterns: Which types also get n8n's built-in POST /credentials/{id}/test. Narrowed to the expirable types, so the run makes no provider calls for the API keys that cannot expire. For those types the built-in test is only a presence check ('access_token' in oauthTokenData), which catches a credential that was never connected or was cleared - the probes do the real work. Widen to [".*"] if you also want revocation detection on the API keys: their types carry a real `test` block, so an OK there does prove the key still works.
_comment_untestable_message_patterns: n8n reports "I could not test this" and "the provider rejected this" through the same {status: Error} response, and only the message tells them apart. These case-insensitive patterns mark the first kind, so the credential is counted as not checked instead of broken. Two real examples from this instance: the n8nApi credential answers "Node not found" because the test node for that type is not installed here, and every httpBearerAuth credential answers "No testing function found for this credential." because generic auth types carry no test block at all - both keys work, and both were being reported as rejected by their provider. Only add a pattern that means n8n never called the provider; anything the provider itself said belongs in the failure count.
_comment_expiry_label_patterns: Case-insensitive regexes marking a word as an expiry label. A date counts as an expiry when one of these appears within label_max_gap characters before it, so "expires 2026-08-01", "caducidad: 15/09/2026" and "renew by 2026-12-01" are all picked up while "created 2024-01-01" is not. Defaults cover English and Spanish; add your own rather than replacing the list if you only want to extend it.
_comment_non_expiry_label_patterns: The opposite: words that mean a nearby date is not a deadline. "Created 2024-03-01 legacy webhook" is a birthday, and reporting it as expired 800 days ago would be worse than saying nothing. Whichever kind of label sits closest before a date decides what that date means; a date with no label either way falls back to accept_bare_iso_dates.
_comment_accept_bare_iso_dates: With no label, an ISO date in the name (2026-08-01) is still taken as the expiry, because nothing else in a credential name looks like that. Ambiguous forms such as 01/08/2026 always need a label - the difference between 1 August and 8 January is not worth guessing.
_comment_day_first: How to read the 4-digit-last form: true means 03/08/2026 is 3 August (Europe), false means 8 March (US). The 4-digit-first form is always year-month-day regardless.
_comment_bands: days_left thresholds, inclusive, nested (critical <= urgent <= warn). Below 0 is EXPIRED. Only credentials inside warn_within_days are reported at all.
_comment_notify_when_clean: false keeps the daily 08:00 run silent when nothing is expiring, so the message only ever lands when it needs a reaction. Set true while tuning to confirm the workflow is actually running.
_comment_report_untracked: Lists credentials with no date in their name and no type rule at the bottom of the digest. This is the nudge that gets the dates written down in the first place - turn it off only once every credential is either dated, covered by a type lifetime, or ignored.
_comment_slack_mention: Prepended to the message only when something is EXPIRED, CRITICAL or BROKEN. Use "<!here>" or "<@U01234567>"; empty means never mention.
_comment_type_lifetime_days: For credential types whose tokens expire on a fixed clock with no refresh, so the deadline can be derived instead of typed: days of validity counted from the credential's updatedAt, which is the moment it was last re-authenticated. This is policy about a type - the same number for everyone using that type - not information about one of your credentials, so nothing here goes stale when a credential is renamed, added or deleted. Only list types that die for good: an OAuth2 credential that silently refreshes itself has no deadline worth reporting, and listing it would fire a false alarm on every run. Keys are n8n credential type names (the `type` field in GET /credentials).
_comment_why_not_read_from_n8n: n8n itself knows the LinkedIn number - the credential wizard shows "Standard LinkedIn apps issue access tokens valid for 60 days and do not return a refresh token" - but that text is a notice property's displayName, and the only endpoint that serves it (/types/credentials.json) needs a browser session rather than an API key, while the public schema endpoint copies property names without their text. Scraping it would mean logging in from the workflow and regexing 402 credential types to recover a single number: exactly 1 of them states a lifetime at all. So the 60 is copied here from that notice, by hand, once.
_comment_lifetime_caveat: A derived date assumes updatedAt is when the token was issued. Re-saving a credential without reconnecting it also bumps updatedAt, which silently pushes the deadline out by a full lifetime - the digest says so on any finding that used a lifetime rule. Shorten the number here if you want a safety margin: 55 instead of 60 warns five days early.
_comment_ignore_name_patterns: Case-insensitive regexes matched against the credential name. Anything matching is counted as ignored and never reported, including in the untracked list. For credentials with no expiry mechanism at all - a local service, an in-cluster password rotated by its helm release. Kept as patterns rather than names so it does not become an inventory: prefer a convention you can match, e.g. suffix those credentials with "(no expiry)".
